finding: The §4 repair answered round 2's derived-value findings (ax-economist store-what-could-be-derived, implementer reset-of-a-derived-value) by rewriting the mechanism from a record-time reset to an output-time truncation, and in doing so added one clause that falsifies §2.1's table and §7 test 4 -- the release's entire quantitative case. The old text was prospective: 'When tp audit --record sees a spec_hash different from the previous round's, it resets consecutive_clean to zero.' The new text is 'stop that walk at the first spec_hash boundary -- zero stored bytes, idempotent under RecordRound's rewrite path, and RETROACTIVE OVER ROUNDS ALREADY ON DISK'. Measured against the exact corpus §2.1 and test 4 name -- spec/.tp-review/0.35.0/state.json plus audit-round-1..9.ndjson -- the nine recorded v0.35.0 rounds carry eight distinct spec_hash values (r1=r2 a46f45c6, r3 c06544ea, r4 50be1428, r5 2dd780c6, r6 6f42a8eb, r7=r8 1259a4af, r9 54e031e6). Simulating both predicates with audit_clean_rounds:2: today blocking converges at round 3 and all at round 9, which is what §2.1's row and test 4 assert. With §4's retroactive truncation applied, blocking converges at round 8 and all NEVER converges -- the only two clean rounds, r8 and r9, are separated by a spec_hash boundary, so the streak the `all` cell depends on cannot exist. So this release contains a section whose mechanism, applied to this release's own replay fixture, changes 'round 3 / round 9' to 'round 8 / never'. That destroys the headline economic claim too: 'six rounds of a nine-round phase spent on a population that was 93% advisory' becomes one round saved. Nothing in the spec says the replay runs with §4 disabled, and §7 test 4 says the replay 'reproduces the recorded history exactly', which under the shipped pair it does not.
suggestion: Either drop 'retroactive over rounds already on disk' and keep §4 prospective (the pre-repair form, which is what makes §2.1 and test 4 true), or keep retroactivity and re-measure §2.1's whole table under the composed rule and rewrite test 4's expected values. If test 4 is deliberately a §2-only replay with §4 switched off, say so in test 4 and drop 'reproducing the recorded history exactly', because the shipped binary will not reproduce it. Add a §7 test that composes the two sections, since the composition is where the release contradicts itself.

finding: The take-back paragraph 17d3007 added ends: 'It takes it back: --check reads the same predicate as --record, and §7 GAINS THE TEST that pins them equal.' §7 gained nothing. Verified with `git diff 9864b00 HEAD -- spec/0.37.0.md`: neither f9295e2 nor 17d3007 touched §7, and the eight test lines are byte-identical to the round-1 and round-2 snapshots. Not one of them mentions --status, --check, or an exit code; tests 1-4 are about audit_converge_on resolution and the finding count, 5 about dispositions, 6-8 about the streak reset. The commit message of 17d3007 asserts the same thing ('sec 7 gains the test pinning the two predicates equal'), so the claim is recorded twice and true nowhere. This is the third consecutive round in which §7 is named as covering a requirement it does not cover: round 2 filed untested-normative-section against the sink validation, the repair withdrew that mechanism and immediately wrote a new promise into §7 without touching §7. A decomposer reading §2.0a will not write the test, because §2.0a says it is already there.
suggestion: Add the test to §7: under blocking, a round whose only surviving non-PASS rows are warning/info makes `tp audit --status --check` exit 0, and the same round under all exits 1; and a round carrying one error row exits 1 under both. Until that line exists in §7, change §2.0a to state the requirement ('§7 must gain a test that pins them equal') rather than reporting it as done.

finding: Round 2's requirement-lost-with-the-section finding said the --check requirement sat in no release. 17d3007 answered it by putting it in TWO, in two incompatible forms, and left this release routing it to the other one. Inside 0.37.0: §2.0a says 'It takes it back: --check reads the same predicate as --record', while §5 -- unchanged -- still lists 'the --check divergence' as one of three sections that left this release and closes 'They are spec/0.46.0.md §8, §8a and §8b'. So the same document both claims and disclaims it. Across the two files it is worse than a duplicate, because the two statements are not the same requirement and disagree on the case that motivated them. spec/0.46.0.md §8 still carries, after 17d3007's edit, 'The candidate shapes, NEITHER CHOSEN HERE: a role-scoped convergence set (converge_roles, defaulting to the conformance role) ... or a --check that reports the shipping predicate itself -- conformance-role streak plus no-FAIL', and it still carries a normative test: 'a fixture where the conformance role is clean for required_clean_rounds running while another role has open non-FAIL rows MUST REACH EXIT 0'. 0.37.0's rule is severity-scoped and role-blind; 0.46.0's surviving test is role-scoped and severity-blind. Take 0.46.0 §8's own fixture and give the other role an error-severity open row: 0.37.0 §2.0a requires exit 1, 0.46.0 §8 requires exit 0. Whichever ships second silently reverses the other. 17d3007 also left §8's heading as 'What this release must decide' over a paragraph that now says the deciding moved elsewhere, and left the requirement's test in a release whose §9 Non-Goal 1 is 'No new mechanism.'
suggestion: Pick one owner and make the other side a pure pointer. If 0.37.0 owns it, delete '--check divergence' from §5's list of three and from §5's closing sentence, and strip 0.46.0 §8 down to the observation plus its table -- moving the candidate shapes and the exit-0 fixture test into 0.37.0 §2.0a/§7, where they can be reconciled with the severity predicate. If 0.46.0 owns it, revert §2.0a's take-back. Do not leave 'reads the same predicate as --record' and 'conformance role clean while another role has open rows must reach exit 0' standing in two specs.

finding: f9295e2 withdrew the mechanism that discharged §2's stated precondition and kept the precondition, and kept the default that rests on it. The withdrawal paragraph is replaced by: 'before blocking may gate, the severity a row carries must be checkable by something other than the row's author, and the 67 recorded rows must have a stated disposition. Four incompatible answers to the second exist and THIS SECTION PICKS NONE OF THEM.' Fourteen lines later §2 still ends '**Default.** blocking'. So the release ships as its default the exact gating mode its own section forbids until two conditions are met, and then declines to meet either. Non-Goal 3, edited in the same commit, closes the only route back: 'Any future proposal that makes --record refuse a row is a different release, and this one must gate on what is already recorded or not gate at all.' Nothing else in the release makes a severity checkable by a non-author -- §7 has no test for it and §2 says so. Before the repair this was coherent: the section asserted a precondition and shipped a mechanism to satisfy it (the round-1 draft) or asserted no precondition at all (the pre-round-1 draft). After the repair the precondition is live, unsatisfied, and unsatisfiable within this release. Round 2 asked for the false safety argument to be removed; removing the argument without removing or discharging the obligation it supported is answering a finding by deletion.
suggestion: Decide the default against the precondition rather than beside it. Either weaken the precondition to something this release can meet ('a severity is checkable by the next round's re-read, which is the check this loop already performs' -- which is what the scope/severity paragraph now argues), or ship `all` as the default and make `blocking` the documented opt-in until a later release makes severity checkable. Do not leave 'before blocking may gate, X must hold', 'this section picks none of them', and 'Default. blocking' in the same section.

finding: Round 2's repaired-claim-contradicts-unrepaired-summary asked for §2.1's closing paragraphs to be rewritten to the 2-of-2 reading. The repair rewrote four words and left the retracted framing standing inside the same sentence and in the sentence after it. Current text: 'So the honest reading is not that blocking is wrong but that **the two cycles AGREE AGAINST IT on the only question that matters, and ONE SAMPLE EACH WAY is not a policy.** What the release owes is that THE DISAGREEMENT is visible'. 'One sample each way' is the 1-1 split, and the immediately preceding paragraph -- added by the same commit -- is titled 'The 1-1 split this paragraph used to rest on is WITHDRAWN'. So the withdrawn claim is restated as the second half of the sentence that withdraws it, and again as 'the disagreement' one clause later. Only the two words 'disagree'/'agree against it' were changed; the two dependent phrases were not. This is the identical failure round 2 recorded at this location, at a smaller scale: the edit landed on the clause the finding quoted and stopped there. Two further remnants of the same framing survive in the section: the heading is still 'What the default would have cost, measured in BOTH DIRECTIONS' and line 171 still opens 'v0.35.0 is the case FOR the release' while the new paragraph nine lines below scores v0.35.0 as a cycle blocking would have shipped an error row over.
suggestion: Rewrite the closing sentence whole rather than swapping its verb: 'Both cycles score against the default on the one question that matters, and two samples the same way is not a policy either.' Then delete 'What the release owes is that the disagreement is visible' or restate it as 'the release owes that the evidence against its own default is visible', retitle §2.1 (the measurement now runs one direction), and reword line 171 so 'the case for the release' is distinguished from 'the case for the default' -- v0.35.0 is still the former and is no longer the latter.

finding: §4 was rewritten this round into a different mechanism with two new normative constraints, and §7 -- which is what decomposition turns into acceptance -- was not touched, so its three streak tests now pin the mechanism §4 replaced and none of them reaches what §4 added. Test 6 reads 'tp audit --record with a spec_hash differing from the previous round RESETS consecutive_clean to zero and REPORTS THE RESET on the machine-readable surface', which is the pre-repair record-time form verbatim; under the new text there is no reset event to report, because consecutive_clean 'is not stored: it is derived at output time by engine.ConsecutiveClean' and the change is a truncation of that walk. An implementer satisfying test 6 literally writes a stored reset flag, which is the design §4 now rejects. Neither of §4's two new constraints has a test: retroactivity over rounds already on disk (which §4 claims 'makes §7 test 7 true by construction' -- but test 7 is unchanged and asserts only that no round is deleted or rewritten, which is a weaker property than retroactive recomputation), and the collision constraint 'Changing the walk changes BOTH PHASES unless the reset is applied by the audit caller, and Non-Goal 4 says this release does not touch review.' That second one is the only thing keeping Non-Goal 4 true, it names a shared helper by file and line (review_status.go:91), and nothing in §7 asserts that review's --status streak is unchanged after the edit. It is exactly the kind of shared-helper regression a guard test catches and prose does not.
suggestion: Rewrite test 6 to the derived form ('a status/record payload computed over rounds whose spec_hash changes reports consecutive_clean 0, with no stored reset flag'), add a test that review's --status consecutive_clean over a review corpus spanning a spec_hash change is unchanged by this release, and add one that recomputes the streak over rounds already on disk so retroactivity is asserted rather than claimed.

finding: The paragraph f9295e2 inserted opens '**Two corrections this sentence needed, both from round 2.**' Counted from spec/.tp-review/0.37.0/review-r2-*.ndjson, round 2 filed five substantive findings against §2.0a: undeclared-invariant-reversal (architect, high), contract-reversal-unrecorded (implementer, high), dangling-cross-ref-after-deletion (regression, high), stale-intra-spec-reference / stale-cross-reference / dangling-section-pointer (architect, implementer, tester -- medium, the same defect from three roles), and uncounted-quantifier (regression, low). The paragraph addresses the first two groups. The third is still wrong nine lines below it, in this same section: '**v0.36.0's rounds 12 and 13 produced TWO error-severity findings**'. Measured from spec/.tp-review/0.36.0/audit-round-12.ndjson and -13.ndjson, round 12 carries 2 non-PASS rows both severity error and round 13 carries 3 of which 2 are error -- four error rows across the two rounds, not two. So a repair that asserts exhaustiveness over the round's corrections passes over an uncounted quantifier and asserts an uncounted quantifier in the same breath. CLAUDE.md names this as the class that rots silently: a claim of exhaustiveness over a set the author did not enumerate.
suggestion: Drop the count: 'Corrections this paragraph needed, from round 2:' and list them. Fix the caveat to 'four error-severity rows across rounds 12 and 13' -- or, if the intent is distinct defects rather than rows, say so and give the defect count, since the caveat's whole force is that a severity gate would have stopped a cycle that still held real defects.

finding: §5's third bullet is the stated reason the split happened: 'The three added ~100 of 288 lines to a release whose remainder (§2, §3, §4) has mechanisms and tests today, pushing it ACROSS THE LENGTH THRESHOLD this repository measured as the strongest single predictor of cycle cost.' Measured: `git show 9864b00^:spec/0.37.0.md | wc -l` is 287 lines, the round-2 snapshot after the split is 229, and the file today is 306. The two repair commits added 77 lines and put the release 19 lines PAST the length the removal was performed to escape, while §5 still stands claiming the length problem was solved by removing content. Every line of the growth is review-narrative rather than mechanism: the four numbered refutations, the withdrawal paragraph, the scope/severity re-derivation, the two-corrections paragraph, the take-back, the 1-1 withdrawal, §3's two new paragraphs, §4's two, and Non-Goal 3's addendum. §2, §3 and §4 gained no new mechanism in this round -- §2 lost one, §3 says its mechanism 'cannot reach the case that motivates it' and picks no replacement, §4 swapped one. So the release is now longer than the version that was split for length while carrying strictly fewer decided mechanisms than it did then. Round 2's architect filed rationale-not-achieved (low) against this bullet; it is measurably worse this round, not better.
suggestion: Either delete §5's length bullet (the reason no longer holds and a false rationale is worse than none), or make it true by cutting the review narrative back to its conclusions. The refutations, withdrawals and 'an earlier draft said' passages belong in the round records under spec/.tp-review/0.37.0/, which already hold them; the spec should carry the surviving claim and, at most, one line saying what was tried and refuted.

finding: §2.0a's take-back states a parity as settled that §3, in the same commit, states cannot be settled yet. §2.0a: 'It takes it back: --check reads the same predicate as --record.' §3: 'clean is stamped at record time (audit_record.go:71, :208) and ConsecutiveClean walks the STORED FLAGS, while --resolve writes the disposition into the round file afterwards ... Either audit's clean flag is recomputed LIVE from rows, the way review's twin already does (review_status.go:91), or the disposition has to survive into the next round's input -- and THIS RELEASE HAS TO PICK ONE.' It picks neither. But --record stamps a flag and --status/--check reads flags, so whether the two commands can read 'the same predicate' at all is precisely the stored-versus-live question §3 leaves open: under the stored form they cannot (a --check run after audit_converge_on changes, or after a --resolve, reads a flag computed under the old rule), and under the live form they can. §4 then makes it three-way, because its truncation is stated as a change to the ConsecutiveClean walk -- the stored-flag reader. So three sections of this release depend on one decision, each describes it differently, and none makes it. Round 2's implementer (stored-vs-live-clean-predicate, critical) and ax-economist (cached-verdict-vs-live-predicate, high) both filed against this; the repair recorded the problem in §3 and then wrote a new dependency on the unmade decision into §2.0a.
suggestion: Make the decision once, in §3, and state it as the release's foundation: audit's clean verdict is recomputed live from the round's rows at every read, the way review_status.go:91 already does. Then §2.0a's parity, §4's truncation and §7 test 4's replay all follow from it. If it cannot be decided this round, §2.0a must not assert the parity as taken back.

finding: Round 2 filed stale-directional-reference against §2's lead paragraph: it ends 'it is the reason THE SINK VALIDATION ABOVE is a precondition rather than a nicety', while the sink validation was described below it, not above. The repair did not fix the direction and instead deleted the referent: f9295e2 withdrew the sink validation entirely and Non-Goal 3, edited in the same commit, now forbids it ('Any future proposal that makes --record refuse a row is a different release'). So the sentence no longer points in the wrong direction -- it points at a mechanism this release has ruled out, three paragraphs below its own retraction. Nothing above line 30 mentions sink validation; §1 does not. The cost is not only the dangling pointer: this paragraph is where the release's strongest measured result lives (the 2-of-2 score against the default), and its stated consequence -- the only thing the measurement is said to imply -- is now a mechanism the release forbids. The measurement therefore supports nothing, and a reader who accepts it is left with no stated reason not to drop the field, which the same sentence pre-emptively denies ('it is not a reason to drop the field') without giving the replacement reason.
suggestion: Rewrite the closing clause to name what the 2-of-2 score actually implies now that sink validation is gone -- e.g. 'it is the reason the default is the one decision here with a recorded argument against it, and the reason §2.1 states the argument rather than burying it'. Then sweep §2 for the other references to the withdrawn draft, since the paragraph that withdrew it now sits below a paragraph that still assumes it shipped.

finding: §1's closing sentence is unchanged since before the split and still scopes the release to two things: 'This release gives audit the two things review already has: a severity-aware convergence policy, and a reason to distrust a streak that spans a changed spec.' The release now ships four: audit_converge_on (§2), the disposition exclusion (§3, which is neither of the two named and pre-dates the split), the spec-change streak reset (§4), and -- added this round by 17d3007 -- --check/--record predicate parity (§2.0a). Round 2's implementer raised the undercount at §6; the repair added a fourth deliverable and left §1 saying two. A decomposer who reads §1 for scope, which is what an overview is for, writes tasks for two of the four.
suggestion: Enumerate what ships: 'audit_converge_on and the --check parity that makes it gate, a disposition that stops blocking, and a streak that a changed spec ends.' Whatever the final list is, it should match §7's tests one-for-one.

finding: Round 2's ax-economist filed provenance-prose-in-normative-spec (medium) against §5, whose heading is 'What is deliberately not in this release, and WHY IT WAS HERE THREE HOURS AGO'. The repair did not remove the pattern; it propagated it into six more sections. Grepping the current file for review-provenance phrasing returns fourteen lines across §2 ('An earlier draft of this section claimed', 'Both review arms falsified it independently in round 1', 'the first attempt at building it was withdrawn in the round after it was written', 'Round 2 refuted it four ways', 'this section has now produced two mechanisms in two rounds and both were wrong within hours', 'an earlier draft of this paragraph denied it'), §2.0a ('Two corrections this sentence needed, both from round 2'), §2.1 ('The 1-1 split this paragraph used to rest on is withdrawn'), §3 ('round 2 measured why'), §5 and §6 ('the withdrawn sink-validation draft'). This is the class spec/0.43.0.md §2 names with this repository's own numbers -- 43% of v0.35.0's findings sat in text the previous round had just written -- and each of these passages is new surface for the next round to review. It is also self-referential in a way that ages badly: 'three hours ago' and 'within hours' are wall-clock claims in a committed artifact (round 2's ax-economist filed that separately as wall-clock-reference-in-committed-artifact).
suggestion: Keep the surviving claim, move the history to the round records that already hold it. Where a refutation must stay because it prevents the idea being re-proposed, compress it to one line naming the mechanism and the reason it died, the way spec/0.44.0.md handles its four refuted candidates -- not four numbered paragraphs with citations.

finding: Near-miss, self-caught before recording. Reading §4's rewrite I first classified it as a clean win -- it answers round 2's store-what-could-be-derived and reset-of-a-derived-value findings by making the reset a property of the derivation instead of a stored byte, and the clause 'retroactive over rounds already on disk' read to me as reassurance that no migration is needed. The wrong finding would have been the absence of one: 'no regression at §4; the mechanism swap is a pure implementation-cost improvement that answers two round-2 findings by design.' What refuted it was refusing to accept the clause on its wording and simulating it against the corpus the same release names -- the nine v0.35.0 rounds carry eight distinct spec_hash values, so retroactive truncation moves blocking from round 3 to round 8 and makes `all` never converge, falsifying §2.1's row and §7 test 4. The general lesson for this role: a repair that answers a finding correctly can still be a regression, and the words that carry it are the ones describing scope ('retroactive', 'shared', 'both phases') rather than the ones describing the mechanism. §4's other new clause -- the shared-helper collision with review's --status -- was found the same way and is filed under test-pins-superseded-mechanism.
suggestion: No spec change from this row. Recorded because the same reflex would have passed over §4 entirely: a section that visibly answers the previous round's findings reads as repaired, and that is precisely when the composed behaviour has to be simulated rather than read.

finding: Near-miss, self-caught before recording. Having measured that §4's retroactive reset breaks the v0.35.0 row, I was about to write the finding as a claim over the whole table -- 'both rows of §2.1 are falsified by §4, so the table has no surviving cell'. Checked the second row before writing: v0.36.0's rounds 2 and 3 share spec_hash f7da0fde, so the blocking round-3 cell survives the truncation unchanged, and the `all` cell was already 'never' with or without it. Only the v0.35.0 row breaks, and only because its two clean rounds, r8 and r9, happen to straddle a hash boundary. The blanket version would have been false in half its extent and would have been refuted in one round by anyone who ran the second row -- the exact shape CLAUDE.md records as the class that keeps getting written: a claim of exhaustiveness over a set the author did not enumerate. It also matters for the repair: the fix is not 'rewrite the table' but 'decide whether §4 composes with the replay', because one cell is already right under both rules.
suggestion: No spec change from this row. Recorded so the merge does not widen the §4 finding when clustering it with the other §2.1 rows: its scope is the v0.35.0 row's two cells and §7 test 4, and the v0.36.0 blocking cell is verified correct under both rules.
